methods.label: Compare opposite sides using translations
methods.explanation:
Assume first that a trapezoid means a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.

Translating by \(x_2\) horizontally and \(y_2\) vertically takes \(O\) to \(Q\) and \(P\) to \(R\). Thus \(OP\) and \(QR\) have equal length and the same direction. Similarly, translating by \(x_1\) horizontally and \(y_1\) vertically takes \(O\) to \(P\) and \(Q\) to \(R\), so \(OQ\) and \(PR\) have equal length and the same direction.

If \(O,P,Q\) are not collinear, these are two different side directions, and both pairs of opposite sides of \(OPRQ\) are parallel. The figure is therefore a parallelogram. For example, \(P=(1,0)\) and \(Q=(0,1)\) give \(R=(1,1)\).

If \(O,P,Q\) are collinear, translating along \(OQ\) keeps their line fixed, so \(R\) also lies on that line. For example, \(P=(1,0)\), \(Q=(2,0)\), and \(R=(3,0)\) give a straight-line figure. The distinctness of \(P,Q,R\) rules out \(P=O\) or \(Q=O\); the permitted case \(R=O\) is also collinear.

These two cases are exhaustive. A nondegenerate figure always has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so it cannot have exactly one such pair. Under the exclusive definition, the answer is \((1)\) or \((2)\) only, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

Under the inclusive definition, a trapezoid has at least one pair of parallel sides. The parallelogram example then also counts as a trapezoid, so all three descriptions can occur and the answer is \(\mathrm{E}\). A unique choice therefore requires the trapezoid convention to be specified.
